lesson.title: The Gustar Family
lesson.subtitle: encantar (me encanta), interesar (me interesa), importar (no me importa), doler (me duele la cabeza)

hook.title: One Blueprint Unlocks a Whole Family of Verbs!
hook.content:
Once you understand how gustar works, you automatically own a whole family of high-frequency Spanish verbs that use the exact same inverted blueprint:
• **encantar** ('to enchant' → 'to love'): **Me encanta la música** ('I love music'), **Me encantan los libros** ('I love books')!
• **importar** ('to matter / be important to'): **No me importa** ('I don't care / It doesn't matter to me')!
• **doler** ('to hurt / ache', o→ue boot verb): **Me duele la cabeza** ('My head hurts / I have a headache', lit. 'To-me hurts the head')!

pattern.title: Why 'Me Encanta' Never Takes 'Mucho'
pattern.content: Because encantar already means 'to love / be delighted by', you say Me encanta el café (whereas with gustar you can say Me gusta mucho el café)!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: it is very important to me / it matters to me
I don't mind / it doesn't matter to me
my head hurts / I have a headache (o→ue)

exercises.target_answer: me encanta la música, me encantan los libros, me importa mucho, no me importa, me duele la cabeza
exercises.meaning: I love music (singular → encanta), I love books (plural → encantan), it is very important to me / it matters to me, I don't mind / it doesn't matter to me, my head hurts / I have a headache (o→ue)
exercises.explanation: All of these verbs put the experiencer in me/te/le/nos and agree with the thing that enchants, matters, or hurts.

exercises.prompt: Spanish 'encantar' ('to delight / cast a spell over') is the exact cognate of which seven-letter English verb meaning 'to charm or delight'?
exercises.meaning: Me encanta el chocolate literally means 'Chocolate enchants me'!
exercises.explanation: Latin incantāre ('to sing a spell upon') gave English enchant and Spanish encantar.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'My head hurts / I have a headache' in Spanish?
exercises.meaning: My head hurts / I have a headache
exercises.explanation: Spanish uses the indirect pronoun me ('to me') + duele ('hurts') + the definite article la cabeza ('the head')!

exercises.idea: say that you love books ('Me encantan los libros')
cues: are enchanting (plural to match libros) → encantan

summary.outcome: Deploy encantar, importar, and doler using the inverted gustar structure.

use_example.german: Me encanta la música, me encantan los libros y hoy me duele la cabeza.
use_example.english: I love music, I love books, and today my head hurts.

summary.takeaway: With body parts (Me duele la cabeza), Spanish uses me/te/le + the definite article (la cabeza) rather than mi/tu/su!
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([26] The Would-World & Subjunctive Preview): unlock the polite conditional (me gustaría, podrías) and the opposite-vowel subjunctive!

encantar.english_meaning: to love, be delighted by (me encanta: I love)
encantar.etymology_derivation: Literally 'it enchants me': me encanta (sg.), me encantan (pl.).

gustar.english_meaning: to be pleasing to (me gusta: I like, lit. it pleases to me)
gustar.shift_rule: Inverted dative experiencer verb (gusta sg. / gustan pl.)
gustar.context_phrase: Me gusta el café y me gustan los libros.
gustar.context_translation: I like coffee and I like books.
gustar.etymology_derivation: Latin gustāre ('to taste') — English gusto and disgust. The thing liked is the grammatical SUBJECT!

gusta.english_meaning: pleases (me gusta + singular noun or infinitive)
gusta.etymology_derivation: With a plural noun, adds -n: me gustan las ciudades.

cabeza.context_translation: My head hurts / I have a headache.
cabeza.etymology_derivation: Used inside el rompecabezas ('the head-breaker' = jigsaw puzzle).

me.etymology_derivation: Walks left of conjugated verbs or hooks onto infinitives.

nos.english_meaning: us, to us, ourselves, each other

le.english_cognate: to him, to her, to usted (dative)
le.english_meaning: to him, to her, to you (usted) (plural: les)
le.shift_rule: Indirect object pronoun (becomes se before lo/la!)
le.context_phrase: Le doy el libro a María.
le.context_translation: I give the book to María.
le.etymology_derivation: Gender-neutral indirect object ('to him / to her / to usted'); turns into se before lo/la/los/las (Se lo doy)!

música.etymology_derivation: Always takes the definite article after gustar: me gusta la música.

no.etymology_derivation: Latin nōn → Spanish no. Negation in Spanish is beautifully direct: place no right before the verb cluster.
